name: India
takeaway: India's fine-particle pollution is among the world's worst, and the people who work outdoors carry the heaviest load while having the least protection.
resident_points: Most Indians live above the WHO guideline, and many above India's own looser standard.|The daily AQI hides the worst hours and most districts have no government monitor.|When Delhi's emergency rules stop work, compensation reaches registered workers far more often than migrants.
main_sources: Dust (dominant for coarse particles); vehicles; household fuels; secondary particles from gases; crop-residue burning (seasonal); industry and brick kilns
source_evidence_note: Source shares differ by city, season and method; see Places
most_exposed: Construction, sanitation and waste workers, vendors, riders, children, residents of informal settlements
who_acts: CPCB, state boards, CAQM (NCR), municipal bodies, welfare boards, Supreme Court, NCAP
interventions_and_experiments: See the six Indian settings and What works
transferable: Airshed plans (Uttar Pradesh); court-enforced worker compensation; school education trial
not_transferable: Delhi's institutions and court oversight are atypical
gaps: Informal earnings losses; monitoring outside metros

name: Bangladesh
takeaway: Bangladesh had the highest average fine-particle pollution of any country in 2023 on one consistent satellite estimate, with brick kilns and traffic among the main local sources around Dhaka.
resident_points: Average PM2.5 in 2023 was about twelve times the WHO guideline, on satellite estimates.|Brick kilns north of Dhaka have been estimated to cause about 40% of fine particles in the firing season; traffic dominates inside the city.|A US$290 million World Bank project approved in 2025 targets monitoring, vehicle testing and electric buses; results are not yet available.
main_sources: Brick kilns (seasonal, north of Dhaka); vehicles; road and construction dust; industry; long-range transport in winter
source_evidence_note: Estimates come from older studies (published 2013); no current official source apportionment was found
most_exposed: Residents of Dhaka and industrial belts; brick-kiln workers; commuters
who_acts: Department of Environment (monitoring and enforcement); World Bank as lender
interventions_and_experiments: Continuous emissions monitoring of industry; vehicle inspection centres; 400 electric buses (approved, not delivered)
transferable: Industrial emissions disclosure linked to enforcement; kiln transition lessons from Bihar and Nepal
not_transferable: Dhaka's kiln belt and river-delta meteorology differ from the Indo-Gangetic plain interior
gaps: Current source apportionment; worker exposure; project results

name: Nepal
takeaway: Air pollution is Nepal's leading risk factor for death and disability, concentrated in the Kathmandu Valley and the Terai, and part of it blows in from across the border.
resident_points: The World Bank estimates about 26,000 premature deaths a year and costs above 6% of GDP.|The bowl-shaped Kathmandu Valley traps pollution; the Terai shares the Indo-Gangetic airshed.|A 2026 World Bank credit aims to help about 400 firms switch to cleaner boilers and furnaces.
main_sources: Industrial and commercial boilers and furnaces (brick and cement); household cooking; transport; open burning; transboundary inflow
source_evidence_note: Sector shares not quantified in sources read
most_exposed: Valley and Terai residents; industrial and brick workers; households cooking with biomass
who_acts: Department of Environment; Department of Industry; World Bank; UK FCDO and Swiss SDC (grant)
transferable: Cleaner-boiler finance combined with technical assistance
not_transferable: Valley topography and cross-border inflow limit what local controls alone can achieve
gaps: How much pollution is local versus transported; household cooking transition

name: Pakistan
takeaway: Winter smog in Lahore and Punjab comes from year-round traffic, waste and industry plus seasonal crop burning on both sides of the border, and the measured share of each depends on the method used.
resident_points: Average PM2.5 in 2023 was about eight times the WHO guideline, on satellite estimates.|Lahore's 2023 inventory puts transport at about 35% of PM2.5 emissions and crop burning at about 33%; the often-quoted 83% transport figure is for all pollutants by weight.|A US$300 million World Bank programme approved in 2025 funds super seeders, electric buses and monitors, with a target, not yet a result, of 35% lower PM2.5 in Lahore Division.
main_sources: Transport; crop-residue burning (seasonal, cross-border); waste burning; industry and brick kilns; household fuels
source_evidence_note: Inventory figures (2020-21 data) differ from other studies; the provincial environment agency disputes some estimates
most_exposed: Lahore residents; outdoor workers; farmers facing burning bans
who_acts: Punjab Environment Protection Department; Punjab real-time monitoring portal; World Bank
interventions_and_experiments: Super seeders; 600 electric buses; regulatory monitors (59 stations by late 2026); fuel testing labs
transferable: Crop-residue alternatives tested in Indian Punjab; monitoring expansion
not_transferable: Cross-border burning means local action cannot control the whole winter episode
gaps: Independent source apportionment; worker and farmer income effects of bans

name: Indonesia
takeaway: Indonesia's national average is lower than South Asia's, but Jakarta is the country's most polluted area and vehicles are its largest measured source, with peat and land fires adding regional haze.
resident_points: Jakarta and nearby Banten top the country's pollution map on satellite estimates.|A Jakarta study found vehicles caused 32-57% of fine particles depending on season.|Community volunteers have measured pollution near a waste incinerator in Surabaya that official monitors did not capture.
main_sources: Vehicles; coal combustion (local hotspots); open burning; construction and road dust; land and peat fires (regional haze)
source_evidence_note: Jakarta study: three sites, two seasons; national haze sources not quantified in sources read
most_exposed: Jakarta residents near traffic; communities near waste facilities; fire-affected regions
who_acts: National and Jakarta environment agencies; Clean Air Fund (since 2025); Breathe Cities partners
interventions_and_experiments: Health-and-economic data for city prioritisation; community monitoring
transferable: Using local health and economic data to prioritise action
not_transferable: Fire-driven haze and island geography differ from South Asian winter inversions
gaps: Haze source quantification; measured results of Jakarta measures

name: Thailand
takeaway: Northern Thailand's most polluted provinces sit in a seasonal burning belt, and the government is now testing payments for crop residue as an alternative to burning.
resident_points: Chiang Rai, Phayao and Nan had the country's highest average fine particles in 2023 on satellite estimates.|The 'Zero Burn to Earn' pilot started in 2026 with private buyers for crop waste; its air-quality effect has not been independently measured.|A research grant (PREDICT-ASIA) is studying how heat and pollution combine to harm health.
main_sources: Seasonal agricultural and forest burning (north); transport and industry (Bangkok)
source_evidence_note: Sector shares not quantified in sources read
most_exposed: Farmers; northern residents in burning season; outdoor workers
who_acts: Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation; Ministry of Agriculture; private buyers
interventions_and_experiments: Residue purchase agreements; burning penalties linked to farm support (reported)
transferable: Residue markets as an alternative to bans (relevant to Indian Punjab and Pakistan)
not_transferable: Upland crop systems and cross-border burning differ from paddy residue in Punjab
gaps: Independent evaluation of residue payments; Bangkok source data

name: Viet Nam
takeaway: Hanoi is Viet Nam's most polluted area, and a new national action plan sets the country's first measurable city targets for cleaner air by 2030.
resident_points: Average PM2.5 in 2023 was about five times the WHO guideline, on satellite estimates.|The 2026-2030 plan targets 20% lower PM2.5 in Hanoi by 2030 compared with 2024.|Sources include transport, industry, energy, construction, waste burning and household fuel.
main_sources: Transport; industry and energy; construction; waste burning; household fuel
source_evidence_note: Listed by WHO/UNDP; shares not quantified in sources read
most_exposed: Hanoi residents; older people and children during winter episodes
who_acts: Government ministries and provinces; WHO and UNDP (technical support)
interventions_and_experiments: National Action Plan 2026-2030 targets (adopted, not yet delivered)
transferable: Outcome targets that can be checked by citizens
not_transferable: Targets are plans; enforcement capacity not assessed
gaps: Delivery and enforcement; source apportionment for Hanoi

name: Philippines
takeaway: Metro Manila and the Benguet highlands are the Philippines' most polluted areas on satellite estimates, and community volunteers have found guideline breaches that official monitors miss.
resident_points: National average PM2.5 in 2023 was about three times the WHO guideline.|Volunteers wearing monitors found WHO guidelines exceeded on 85-100% of days.|An electric-mobility programme is under way; its funding details could not be confirmed from primary pages.
main_sources: Transport; waste burning; other sources not quantified in sources read
source_evidence_note: Sector shares not established in this edition
most_exposed: Commuters and transport workers; communities near waste facilities
who_acts: Department of Trade and Industry; Board of Investments; Clean Air Asia; community groups
transferable: Community monitoring as evidence for local decisions
not_transferable: Island urban form; electric mobility benefits on street-level air not measured
gaps: Source apportionment for Metro Manila; e-mobility programme documents

name: Cambodia
takeaway: Phnom Penh is Cambodia's most polluted area on satellite estimates, and a new project is testing how to manage rice straw without burning it.
resident_points: National average PM2.5 in 2023 was nearly four times the WHO guideline.|A 2026 project led by the International Rice Research Institute addresses rice-straw burning and black carbon.|Its budget and results could not be confirmed.
who_acts: Ministry of Environment; Ministry of Agriculture (agricultural engineering); CCAC; IRRI
transferable: Residue management lessons for paddy regions
not_transferable: Smallholder systems differ from mechanised Punjab
